title: A Verified Core for Tax Administration: Philippine Tax Rules and a Proven Checker in Lean 4
author: Aaron Y. Hernandez
affiliation: Senior High School, Benigno S. Aquino National High School, Philippines
body: Legal systems are increasingly implemented through software, yet scalable methods for translating legal texts into accurate symbolic representations remain underdeveloped [3]. Following neuro-symbolic formalization of United States tax forms [1] and law-specific languages for statutory computation [2], we study Philippine tax law, where the National Internal Revenue Code and its amendments define computational structures of arithmetic, branching, and tabular reasoning [4,5]. We propose a verified Lean 4 core formalizing the TRAIN income tax schedule, late-payment penalties, the ₱3,000,000 VAT threshold, taxpayer tiers, and the 8% optional regime as executable, machine-checked definitions. Our approach establishes two correspondences between law and logic: structural, aligning the statutory bracket schedule with the checker's bracket list, and denotational, proved as soundness and completeness of a certificate checker accepting any engine's line-by-line assessment only if every line implements the statute's computation. We combine kernel-checked proofs (54 theorems, 64 examples, no unproven steps) with mutation tests and a benchmark whose ground truth is agreed by independent Python and Lean implementations. We then evaluate untrusted engines: seven seeded-fault implementations and three large language model sessions, 254 certificates judged only by the verified checker. Although a misreading of the ₱3,000,000 tier boundary passes 30 of 32 cases, the checker rejects it, and no faulty engine produces an accepted wrong total, demonstrating the effectiveness of symbolic verification compared with trusting the computation alone. The encoded specification awaits practitioner review.
references: S. S. Han, Y. Takashima, A. Wei, Z. Li, M. Genesereth,
Law and Order: Tax Law Autoformalization
